orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the December 2, 2021 judgment dismissing the claim against Aldrich following the liability verdict and denial of a new-trial motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Entered judgment dismissing the claim against Aldrich after a defense liability verdict; denied plaintiff's CPLR 4404(a) motion to set aside the verdict and for a new trial.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff testified that she slipped on snow and ice while entering her car after leaving a restaurant in Aldrich's shopping center. The restaurant manager instead recounted a regular customer's report of falling into a hole while exiting her car in the rear lot; employees testified that Aldrich did not inspect its snow-removal contractor's work.

legal_issues.finding: The court held that the jury could consistently find negligent snow/ice removal without finding that negligence a substantial factor in this accident. It did not conclusively choose the hole account as the cause.
The court rejected the CPLR 4404(a) weight-of-the-evidence/new-trial challenge after substantively assessing the relationship between negligence and proximate cause.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff testified about snow/ice, no salt/sand and slipping while entering her car.
The restaurant manager's deposition excerpts recounted a customer's different account; Aldrich employees testified about lack of inspection of contractor work.

quality.notes: This is substantive review of a negligence verdict, despite the post-trial procedural vehicle. One appealed judgment; the new-trial motion is not a second independently appealed order. Competing testimony is preserved without resolving the factual discrepancy. Customer role comes from the manager's account of this incident, not solely the restaurant setting. No exact accident date is stated. The retained snow-removal contractor is not identified as a defendant and no contractor-duty issue is analyzed.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the judgment is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries she allegedly sustained when she slipped and fell on snow and ice in the parking lot of a Dunkin Donuts restaurant located in a shopping center owned by the defendant Aldrich Management Co., LLC (hereinafter Aldrich).

The judgment, upon a jury verdict in favor of the defendant Aldrich Management Co., LLC, on the issue of liability, and upon the denial of the plaintiff's motion pursuant to CPLR 4404 (a) to set aside the jury verdict as contrary to the weight of the evidence and for a new trial, is in favor of the defendant Aldrich Management Co., LLC, and against the plaintiff dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against that defendant.

The plaintiff testified at trial that after leaving the Dunkin Donuts restaurant, she slipped and fell while attempting to get into her car, which was parked in the parking lot on the east side of the building. The plaintiff also testified that at the time of her fall, there was approximately one inch of ice and snow covering the parking lot, and no salt or sand had been applied to the parking lot.

Rivera testified that she learned of this incident when an individual, who was a regular customer, came into the restaurant and stated that she had just fallen into a "big hole" in the rear parking lot as she was getting out of her car.

Testimony was also presented from employees of Aldrich, who indicated that Aldrich did not send a representative to inspect the work of the contractor it retained to clear snow and ice from the parking lot.
At the conclusion of the trial, the jury returned a verdict finding that Aldrich was negligent, but that its negligence was not a substantial factor in bringing about the plaintiff's accident.
Here, contrary to the plaintiff's contention, the issues of negligence and proximate cause were not inextricably interwoven, and the jury's finding was not contrary to the weight of the evidence.

Under the circumstances, the jury could have found that while Aldrich was negligent in failing to adequately clear snow and ice from the parking lot, such negligence was not a substantial factor in causing this occurrence
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the plaintiff's motion pursuant to CPLR 4404 (a) to set aside the jury verdict as contrary to the weight of the evidence and for a new trial.
During the trial, Aldrich's attorney read into the record excerpts of the deposition testimony of Encasnita Rivera, a manager of the subject Dunkin Donuts restaurant.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the August 6, 2020 order granting the relevant branches of two separate defense motions.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted summary judgment dismissing the complaint against both the DJ's International defendants and Aldrich Management.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff fell while descending a restaurant staircase with a box in both hands. His expert attributed the fall to alleged tread, handrail and lighting defects, but the actual fall mechanism was not identified.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established that plaintiff could not identify the fall's cause; the expert's alternative defect theory was speculative and raised no triable issue.
The court found the expert's theory linking alleged New York State Building Code tread/handrail/lighting violations to this fall speculative; it did not establish that no violations existed.
Plaintiff's expert's causation theory was insufficient to raise a triable issue, as it did not distinguish alleged defects from a misstep or loss of balance.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff offered an expert theory of code-related tread, handrail and lighting defects; the court found the causal connection speculative.

quality.notes: Incident-mechanism review: the actual-case description states only a fall descending stairs, not a slip or trip. A generic quoted trip-and-fall rule is not case-specific proof. Reason other denotes this uncertainty, not a definite out-of-scope finding. Lack of causal proof alone does not exclude negligence cases under the codebook. One appealed order resolved two motions; multiple_orders is false. The source calls DJ's entities lessors, so their role is other rather than silently changing it to tenant. Plaintiff's employment/customer status and accident date are unknown.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when he fell while descending a staircase at a restaurant while carrying a box in both hands.

Thereafter, the plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries against the lessors of the restaurant, DJ's International Buffet, Inc., and DJ's International Buffet, Inc., doing business as DJ's International Bar & Grill (hereinafter together the DJ's International defendants), and the owner of the restaurant, Aldrich Management Co., LLC (hereinafter Aldrich Management).

The order granted that branch of the motion of the defendants DJ's International Buffet, Inc., and DJ's International Buffet, Inc., doing business as DJ's International Bar & Grill, which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them and granted that branch of the separate motion of the defendant Aldrich Management Co., LLC, which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
Here, the defendants met their prima facie burden by establishing that the plaintiff cannot identify the cause of his fall
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a material issue of fact.

The speculative theory offered by the plaintiff's expert that the plaintiff's fall was caused by alleged violations of the New York State Building Code pertaining to an alleged defective tread and handrails on the staircase and improper lighting, rather than a misstep or loss of balance, was insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted those branches of the defendants' respective motions which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the December 5, 2013 order granting defendant summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped and fell in the laundry room of a building attributed to defendant and presumed water caused the fall because her pants were damp. Defendant's supervisor described a clean, dry floor on three checks that day, while plaintiff's expert attributed alleged slipperiness to the ventilation system.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established noncreation; plaintiff's expert's ventilation-system theory failed to raise a triable issue.
The court found defendant lacked notice; its claims representative reported no water complaints during the preceding three months.
The court found defendant lacked notice; the supervisor's affidavit described three same-day inspections finding the floor clean and dry.
The opinion considered plaintiff's presumed-water account and the expert's failure to connect testing or observed wetness to the accident conditions and precise fall area.

The expert did not sufficiently replicate accident-day conditions, lacked ventilation expertise, and did not identify wetness at the precise fall location; the affidavit failed to defeat summary judgment.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff testified that she saw no water where she fell and inferred water from damp pants.
Janitorial-supervisor affidavit reported three same-day checks; the claims representative reported no water complaints over three months.
Plaintiff's affidavit proposed a ventilation-related condition based on testing five months later; the court found defects in expertise, replication and spatial specificity.

quality.notes: Private-property status needs review: 'defendant's building' and a defendant-employed janitorial supervisor establish attribution/maintenance but do not expressly establish private ownership, lease or the building's use. No public-housing or residential status is inferred from the corporate name, laundry room or cited cases. The property evidence is retained for human application of the existing rule. Do not treat the corporate defendant alone as proof. Specific inspection/maintenance records are not stated to have been submitted; witness accounts of checks and schedules are coded as testimony. Plaintiff's role and accident date are unknown.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Sharon A.M. Aarons, J.), entered December 5, 2013, which granted defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Defendant established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by showing that it neither created nor had notice of the condition that allegedly caused plaintiff to slip and fall in the laundry room of defendant's building.

Defendant submitted evidence including plaintiff's testimony that she did not see any water on the floor in the area where she fell, and that she presumed that she slipped on water because her pants were damp.

Defendant also submitted an affidavit from its janitorial supervisor, who stated that in accordance with the established maintenance schedule, he checked the laundry room floor three times on the day of the accident and found that it was clean and dry
Furthermore, defendant's claims representative stated that for the three-month period before the date of the accident, no complaints were lodged relating to water on the floor of the laundry room.
In opposition, plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.

Plaintiff's reliance on the affidavit of her expert, who stated that the design and construction of the laundry room ventilation system created a dangerous, slippery condition on the floor, is misplaced because as noted by the motion court, the expert did not demonstrate that the testing he performed sufficiently replicated the conditions in the laundry room on the day of the accident, which was five months earlier
The expert also lacked the expertise to offer his opinion with respect to the ventilation system in the laundry room

Even assuming plaintiff's expert was qualified to render an expert opinion, it is noted that his affidavit states that he touched the laundry room floor with his hand and found that it was "wet and damp." However, he did not state that the floor was wet in the area where plaintiff fell, and, "an expert's examination of a part of the general area is insufficient to preclude summary judgment"

orders.description: Plaintiffs' appeal from the June 13, 2008 defense judgment after a liability trial.
orders.trial_court_action: Entered judgment effectively dismissing the complaint following a defense verdict on liability.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiffs presented evidence that decedent slipped on ice on property attributed to defendants. Defendants presented a competing account that the injury resulted from a fall at decedent's home.

legal_issues.finding: The trial court improperly replaced a seated juror under CPLR 4106 without evidence of bias; speculative concern about future bias was insufficient. The appellate court ordered a new liability trial without deciding the remaining contentions.

evidence_discussed.description: Both sides presented evidence about the accident location/cause, but this opinion does not identify its form. The juror answered the court's questions about her acquaintance with a defense witness.

quality.notes: Excluded under the procedural-only rule: the appellate analysis resolves juror replacement, not negligence, notice, defect or causation merits. Reversal of a final trial judgment does not by itself establish substantive negligence review. Competing accident accounts are background, not an adjudicated causation issue. The whole disposition is reversed with consequential remand, not remand_only; binary label is null because of scope exclusion. Property is attributed to defendants but private status, legal ownership/control basis, site type and precise location are not specified; exclusion does not depend on resolving that uncertainty. No human adjudication is claimed.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the judgment is reversed, on the law, on the facts, and in the exercise of discretion, with costs, the complaint is reinstated, and the matter is remitted to the Supreme Court, Nassau County, for a new trial on the issue of liability, and a trial on the issue of damages, if warranted.

In an action to recover damages for wrongful death, etc., the plaintiffs appeal from a judgment of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Spinola, J.), entered June 13, 2008, which, upon a *673 jury verdict on the issue of liability in favor of the defendants and against them, is in favor of the defendants and against them, in effect, dismissing the complaint.

At trial, the plaintiffs presented evidence that their decedent, who died after sustaining a severe head injury in a fall, slipped and fell on a patch of ice located upon the defendants’ property. However, the defendants presented certain evidence indicating that the decedent’s injuries were the result of a fall at his home.

The juror explained that she lived in the same neighborhood as the witness, and graduated from high school with her. The juror also indicated that the extent of their relationship was that they would occasionally see each other on the street, say hello, and ask each other how they were doing.
However, defense counsel then made an application, which the plaintiffs’ attorney opposed, for the juror to be replaced with an alternate juror.

Here, however, there was no indication that the juror in question evinced any bias or prejudice against one of the parties. Furthermore, the trial court’s concern that such a bias or prejudice might eventually surface was speculative.
Under these circumstances,- the court should have denied defense counsel’s application, and should not have replaced the juror with an alternate juror
Therefore, the judgment must be reversed, the complaint reinstated, and the matter remitted for a new trial On the issue of liability.
In light of our determination, we do not address the plaintiffs’ remaining contentions.

CPLR 4106 provides that, in a civil case, if, before the final submission of the case to the jury, a seated juror “dies, or becomes ill, or for any other reason is unable to perform his [or her] duty,” the trial court may remove the juror and replace the juror with an alternate juror.

orders.description: Appeal from the July 1, 2009 order denying defendants' summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped and fell on snow-covered ice in a parking lot owned by defendants. The parties' submissions left the timing of the ice accumulation relative to a storm unresolved.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants failed to meet their initial burden to show lack of constructive notice; the court did not conclusively find notice.
Defendants' submissions left a triable issue whether the fall involved storm-time ice or ice accumulated before the storm, so the storm defense did not establish summary-judgment entitlement.

quality.notes: Only the parking lot is described; parking_only records that stated site and does not infer a shopping-center setting from the defendant's name. Specific evidence types, accident date and plaintiff's role are unstated. The pending factual questions do not make the appellate disposition ambiguous.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed with costs.
Memorandum: Plaintiffs commenced this action seeking damages for injuries sustained by Krystal Tonkin (plaintiff) when she slipped and fell on snow-covered ice in a parking lot owned by defendants.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Chautauqua County (James H. Dillon, J.), entered July 1, 2009 in a personal injury action. The order denied the motion of defendants for summary judgment.
Supreme Court properly denied defendants’ motion seeking summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint.

Defendants’ own submissions raise a triable issue of fact whether plaintiff fell “as the result of an icy condition occurring during an ongoing storm or for a reasonable time thereafter” (Solazzo v New York City Tr. Auth., 6 NY3d 734, 735 [2005]), or whether she fell as the result of ice that had accumulated prior to the storm
In addition, defendants failed to meet their initial burden of establishing that they lacked constructive notice of the icy condition
